value.overview: The Ruddy-tailed Flycatcher (Terenotriccus erythrurus) is a small, inconspicuous insect-eating bird of humid tropical forests. It is the only species in its genus and is recognized by its warm reddish-brown tail, olive-brown upperparts, pale underparts, and relatively short bill. It usually stays in dense, shaded vegetation near the forest floor, where it makes short sallies to capture insects. In Costa Rica, it is a resident species associated mainly with humid lowland and foothill forest.
value.classification: The Ruddy-tailed Flycatcher belongs to the family Onychorhynchidae, the royal flycatchers and related becards, within the order Passeriformes. Terenotriccus erythrurus is the only species in its genus.
value.identification: This small flycatcher has olive-brown to brownish upperparts, a distinctly rufous or cinnamon-colored tail, and pale grayish or buff underparts. The throat and breast may show warm buff or cinnamon tones, and the face is subdued rather than strongly patterned. Its compact shape, short bill, reddish tail, and preference for dark understory help separate it from many other forest flycatchers. It is often detected by its voice before it is seen.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from southern Mexico and Central America through much of northern and western South America, generally in humid forest regions. In Costa Rica it is a resident, recorded on both the Caribbean slope and the southern Pacific slope, especially in lowland and foothill rainforest. It favors mature evergreen forest, forest edges with dense shade, second growth near intact forest, ravines, and other damp habitats with thick understory. It is less associated with open farmland or urban areas.
value.migrationStatus: It is generally considered a nonmigratory resident. In Costa Rica, individuals are present year-round rather than being regular seasonal migrants, although local movements may occur in response to food, weather, or habitat conditions.
value.breeding: Reliable information on the breeding biology of the Ruddy-tailed Flycatcher is limited. Like other small forest flycatchers, it is believed to breed during the wetter or seasonally favorable part of the year, when insect food is abundant. Nest placement and parental behavior are not as well documented as those of more conspicuous flycatchers. In Costa Rica, breeding may occur within suitable humid forest, but detailed national information on nesting sites and timing is sparse.
value.dietFeeding: The Ruddy-tailed Flycatcher feeds mainly on small insects and other arthropods. It usually forages from low perches in shaded forest understory, watching quietly before making short, rapid flights to seize prey from the air or vegetation. It may also pick prey from leaves, twigs, or other surfaces. Its unobtrusive behavior and dense habitat make feeding activity difficult to observe, even where the species is present.
value.behavior: This is a quiet, solitary, and secretive forest bird. It commonly remains in the lower and middle understory, perching motionless for extended periods and moving through shaded vegetation with quick, deliberate flights. It is often easier to locate by its call than by sight. Individuals may defend small feeding or breeding territories, and pairs may remain unobtrusive among dense foliage. The species generally avoids exposed perches and open landscapes.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly established, but the species is sufficiently widespread and numerous for a Least Concern assessment.
